entries.c78ab354a891e907b14cf6aa9acfa8b24eb93660: <div eID="gen24404" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen24405" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen24406" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24406" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24405" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen24407" type="x-p"/> The man who separates himself and seeks wisdom. The fool and the wicked man. Deep wisdom. Contention of fools. The talebearer and the slothful. The name of the Lord. Pride and presumption because of riches. Hastiness of spirit. The wounded spirit. The influence of gifts. The lot. The offended brother. The influence of the tongue. A wife a good from God. The true friend. <div eID="gen24407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24408" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen24408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24409" type="x-p"/> Through desire a man, having separated himself - The original is difficult and obscure. The Vulgate, Septuagint, and Arabic, read as follows: "He who wishes to break with his friend, and seeks occasions or pretenses shall at all times be worthy of blame." <div eID="gen24409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24410" type="x-p"/> My old MS. Bible translates, Occasioun seeketh that wil go awei fro a freend: at al tyme he schal ben wariable. <div eID="gen24410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24411" type="x-p"/> Coverdale thus: "Who so hath pleasure to sowe discorde, piketh a quarrel in every thinge." <div eID="gen24411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24412" type="x-p"/> Bible by Barker, 1615: "Fro the desire thereof he will separate himself to seeke it, and occupie himself in all wisdome." Which has in the margin the following note: "He that loveth wisdom will separate himself from all impediments, and give himself wholly to seek it." <div eID="gen24412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24413" type="x-p"/> The Hebrew: לתאוה יבקש נפרד בכל תושיה יתגלע lethaavah yebakkesh niphrad, bechol tushiyah yithgalla. The nearest translation to the words is perhaps the following: "He who is separated shall seek the desired thing, (i.e., the object of his desire), and shall intermeddle (mingle himself) with all realities or all essential knowledge." He finds that he can make little progress in the investigation of Divine and natural things, if he have much to do with secular or trifliing matters: he therefore separates himself as well from unprofitable pursuits as from frivolous company, and then enters into the spirit of his pursuit; is not satisfied with superficial observances, but examines the substance and essence, as far as possible, of those things which have been the objects of his desire. This appears to me the best meaning: the reader may judge for himself.
entries.b2b5f2379242a85436016e4839ace11dd954ee5f: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen24413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24414" type="x-p"/> But that his heart may discover itself - It is a fact that most vain and foolish people are never satisfied in company, but in showing their own nonsense and emptiness. But this verse may be understood as confirming the view already given of the preceding, and may be translated thus: "But a fool doth not delight in understanding, though it should even manifest itself:" so I understand כי אם בהתגלות ki im behithgalloth. The separated person seeks understanding in every hidden thing, and feels his toil well repaid when he finds it, even after the most painful and expensive search: the other regards it not, though its secret springs should be laid open to him without toil or expense.
entries.5794a28653c1d3a4fddaa1716ab07f71d1571830: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen24414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24415" type="x-p"/> When the wicked cometh, etc. - would it not be better to read this verse thus? "When the wicked cometh contempt cometh; and with ignominy cometh reproach." A wicked man is despised even by the wicked. He who falls under ignominy falls under reproach.
entries.243e61eac611c96a122406d18e613e03c0df876a: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen24415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24416" type="x-p"/> The words of a man's mouth - That is, the wise sayings of a wise man are like deep waters; howsoever much you pump or draw off, you do not appear to lessen them. <div eID="gen24416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24417" type="x-p"/> The well-spring of wisdom - Where there is a sound understanding, and a deep, well-informed mind, its wisdom and its counsels are an incessant stream, מקור חכמה mekor chochmah, "the vein of wisdom," ever throwing out its healthy streams: but מקור חיים mekor chaiyim, "the vein of Lives," is the reading of eight of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS., and is countenanced by the Septuagint, πηγη ζωης, "the fountain of life." And so the Arabic. This is the more likely to be the true reading, because the figure of the heart propelling the blood through the great aorta, to send it to all parts of the animal system, is a favourite with Solomon, as it was with his father, David. See the note on <reference osisRef="Psa.36.9">Psa 36:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Pro.10.11">Pro 10:11</reference>, etc.
entries.537d68a9c9bfb58091a1dfb8a2751c202677362e: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen24417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24418" type="x-p"/> To accept the person of the wicked - We must not, in judicial cases, pay any attention to a man's riches, influence, friends, offices, etc., but judge the case according to its own merits. But when the wicked rich man opposes and oppresses the poor righteous, then all those things should be utterly forgotten.
entries.f85d7f90457b347434b01e7ddc22f5a7889ba76d: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen24418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24419" type="x-p"/> The words of a tale-bearer - דברי נרגן dibrey nirgan, "the words of the whisperer," the busy-body, the busy, meddling croaker. Verba bilinguis, "the words of the double-tongued." - Vulgate. The wordes of the twisel tunge - Old MS. Bible. "The words of a slanderer." - Coverdale. <div eID="gen24419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24420" type="x-p"/> The words of a deceiver, the fair-spoken, deeply-malicious man, though they appear soft and gracious, are wounds deeply injurious. <div eID="gen24420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24421" type="x-p"/> The original word is כמתלהמים kemithlahamim; they are as soft or simple, or undesigning. But Schultens gives another meaning. He observes that lahamah in Arabic signifies to "swallow down quickly or greedily." Such words are like dainties, eagerly swallowed, because inviting to the taste; like gingerbread, apparently gilded over, though with Dutch leaf, which is a preparation of copper; or sweetmeats powdered over with red candied seeds, which are thus formed by red lead; both deeply ruinous to the tender bowels of the poor little innocents, but, because of their sweetness and inviting color, greedily swallowed down. This makes a good reading, and agrees with the latter clause of the verse, "they go down into the innermost parts of the belly."
entries.9dca756e6a6b8422981a761de8b7f350acd0ce4d: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen24421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24422" type="x-p"/> He also that is slothful - A slothful man neglects his work, and the materials go to ruin: the master, he destroys the materials. They are both destroyers.
entries.0b7b360dd786919f0f92d61fdf066c5bc8153ca0: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen24422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24423" type="x-p"/> The name of the Lord is a strong tower - The name of the Lord may be taken for the Lord himself; he is a strong tower, a refuge, and place of complete safety, to all that trust in him. What a strong fortress is to the besieged, the like is God to his persecuted, tempted, afflicted followers.
entries.0dd1d7dad51556d403527300db783f9f68313fd5: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen24423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24424" type="x-p"/> The rich man's wealth - See <reference osisRef="Pro.10.15">Pro 10:15</reference>.
entries.c2beb3510627802dcf4e410315dfcab02835b77a: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen24424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24425" type="x-p"/> Before destruction - See on <reference osisRef="Pro.11.2">Pro 11:2</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Pro.16.18">Pro 16:18</reference> (note).
entries.0664a01177ca55ea270896c0f1251caf6492e3d2: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen24425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24426" type="x-p"/> He that answereth a matter - This is a common case; before a man can tell out his story, another will begin his. Before a man has made his response, the other wishes to confute piecemeal, though he has had his own speech already. This is foolishness to them. They are ill-bred. There are many also that give judgment before they hear the whole of the cause, and express an opinion before they hear the state of the case. How absurd, stupid, and foolish!
entries.be8ef94f908810069040768bc6545ba4e4e6d904: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen24426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24427" type="x-p"/> The spirit of a man will sustain - A man sustains the ills of his body, and the trials of life, by the strength and energy of his mind. But if the mind be scoundrel, if this be cast down, if slow-consuming care and grief have shot the dagger into the soul, what can then sustain the man? Nothing but the unseen God. Therefore, let the afflicted pray. A man's own spirit has, in general, sufficient fortitude to bear up under the unavoidable trials of life; but when the conscience is wounded by sin, and the soul is dying by iniquity, who can lift him up? God alone; for salvation is of the Lord.
entries.7eebd4da4305f4a052c89f50a4f763870a1cf987: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen24427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24428" type="x-p"/> A man's gift maketh room for him - It is, and ever has been, a base and degrading practice in Asiatic countries, to bring a gift or present to the great man into whose presence you come. Without this there is no audience, no favor, no justice. This arose from the circumstance that men must not approach the altar of God without an offering. <div eID="gen24428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24429" type="x-p"/> Potentates, wishing to be considered as petty gods, demanded a similar homage: - <div eID="gen24429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24430" type="x-p"/> Munera, crede mihi, capiunt hominesquedeosque; <div eID="gen24430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24431" type="x-p"/> Placatur donis Jupiter ipse suis. <div eID="gen24431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24432" type="x-p"/> Ovid "Believe me, gifts prevail much with both gods and men: even Jupiter himself is pleased with his own offerings."
entries.24f4505c9c5ebebe119dfe97a4e6a7406761e7cc: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen24432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24433" type="x-p"/> He that is first in his own cause - Any man may, in the first instance, make out a fair tale, because he has the choice of circumstances and arguments. But when the neighbor cometh and searcheth him, he examines all, dissects all, swears and cross-questions every witness, and brings out truth and fact.
entries.e32a2e01d11e0578f722f51b6fa4a5e1f3812887: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen24433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24434" type="x-p"/> The lot causeth contentions to cease - See note on <reference osisRef="Pro.16.33">Pro 16:33</reference>.
entries.8c4617d55c8d43b68d284a5fc5b5b673ecaf12b6: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen24434" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24435" type="x-p"/> A brother offended is harder to be won than a strong city - Almost all the versions agree in the following reading: "A brother assisted by a brother, is like a fortified city; and their decisions are like the bars of a city." Coverdale is both plain and terse: "The unitie of brethren is stronger then a castell, and they that holde together are like the barre of a palace." The fable of the dying father, his sons, and the bundle of faggots, illustrates this proverb. Unity among brethren makes them invincible; small things grow great by concord. If we take the words according to the common version, we see them express what, alas! we know to be too generally true: that when brothers fall out, it is with extreme difficulty that they can be reconciled. And fraternal enmities are generally strong and inveterate.
entries.437e416419ff6499b3c11fa42a98b29e422ef08c: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen24435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24436" type="x-p"/> With the fruit of his mouth - Our own words frequently shape our good or evil fortune in life.
entries.6106b5414cd30c755b2b2ec85323c6513cbf4a42: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen24436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24437" type="x-p"/> Death and life are in the power of the tongue - This may apply to all men. Many have lost their lives by their tongue, and some have saved their lives by it: but it applies most forcibly to public pleaders; on many of their tongues hangs life or death.
entries.35cd1f21b4f3f774b9554e918dee8e964afa0023: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen24437" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24438" type="x-p"/> Whoso findeth a wife findeth a good thing - Marriage, with all its troubles and embarrassments, is a blessing from God; and there are few cases where a wife of any sort is not better than none, because celibacy is an evil; for God himself hath said, "It is not good for man to be alone." None of the versions, except the Chaldee, are pleased with the naked simplicity of the Hebrew text, hence they all add good: "He that findeth a Good wife findeth a good thing;" and most people, who have not deeply considered the subject, think the assertion, without this qualification, is absurd. Some copies of the Targum, and apparently one of Kennicott's MSS., have the addition טובה tobah, good; but this would be an authority too slender to justify changing the Hebrew text; yet Houbigant, Kennicott, and other able critics argue for it. The Septuagint is not satisfied without an addition: "But he who puts away a good wife, puts away a good thing: and he that retains an adulteress, is a fool and wicked." In this addition the Vulgate, Syriac, and Arabic, agree with the Septuagint. The Hebrew text as it stands, teaches a general doctrine by a simple but general proposition: "He that findeth a wife findeth a good thing." So St. Paul: "Marriage is honorable in all." Had the world been left, in this respect, to the unbridled propensities of man, in what a horrible state would society have been - if indeed society could have existed, or civilization have taken place - if marriage had not obtained among men! As to good wives and bad wives, they are relatively so, in general; and most of them that have been bad afterwards, have been good at first; and we well know the best things may deteriorate, and the world generally allows that where there are matrimonial contentions, there are faults on both sides.
entries.4285ca8cd2b0050e24fe8eaa5d38cef888d88535: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen24438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24439" type="x-p"/> A man that hath friends must show himself friendly - Love begets love; and love requires love as its recompense. If a man do not maintain a friendly carriage, he cannot expect to retain his friends. Friendship is a good plant; but it requires cultivation to make it grow. <div eID="gen24439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24440" type="x-p"/> There is a kind of factitious friendship in the world, that, to show one's self friendly in it, is very expensive, and in every way utterly unprofitable: it is maintained by expensive parties. feasts, etc., where the table groans with dainties, and where the conversation is either jejune and insipid, or calumnious; backbiting, talebearing, and scandal, being the general topics of the different squads in company. <div eID="gen24440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24441" type="x-p"/> There is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother - In many cases the genuine friend has shown more attachment, and rendered greater benefits, than the natural brother. Some apply this to God; others to Christ; but the text has no such meaning. <div eID="gen24441" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24442" type="x-p"/> But critics and commentators are not agreed on the translation of this verse. The original is condensed and obscure. אוש רעים להתרועע ish reim lehithroea, or lehithroeang, as some would read, who translate: A man of friends may ring again; i.e., he may boast and mightily exult: but there is a friend, אהב oheb, a lover, that sticketh closer, דבק dabek, is glued or cemented, מאח meach, beyond, or more than, a brother. The former will continue during prosperity, but the latter continues closely united to his friend, even in the most disastrous circumstances. <div eID="gen24442" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24443" type="x-p"/> Hence that maxim of Cicero, so often repeated, and so well known: - <div eID="gen24443" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24444" type="x-p"/> Amicus certus in re incerta cernitur. "In doubtful times the genuine friend is known." <div eID="gen24444" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24445" type="x-p"/> A late commentator has translated the verse thus: - <div eID="gen24445" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24446" type="x-p"/> The man that hath many friends is ready to be ruined: <div eID="gen24446" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24447" type="x-p"/> But there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother. <div eID="gen24447" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24448" type="x-p"/> Holden. "A frende that delyteth in love, doth a man more frendship, and sticketh faster unto him, than a brother." Coverdale. "A man that hath friends ought to show himself friendly for a friend is nearer than a brother." Barker's Bible, 1615. "A man amyable to felowschip, more a freend schal ben thanne a brother." - Old MS. Bible. The two last verses in this chapter, and the two first of the next, are wanting in the Septuagint and Arabic. <div eID="gen24448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24449" type="x-p"/> These are the principal varieties; out of them the reader may choose. I have already given my opinion.  <chapter eID="Prov.18"/> <div eID="gen24449" type="x-p"/>

entries.68a6c70d02e166c0499d98541645de80656a0675: <reference osisRef="Prov.18.1">Pro 18:1</reference> <div eID="gen11304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11305" type="x-p"/> This series of proverbs now turns from the fool to the separatist: <div eID="gen11305" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11306" type="x-p"/> The separatist seeketh after his own pleasure; <div eID="gen11306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11307" type="x-p"/> Against all that is beneficial he showeth his teeth. <div eID="gen11307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11308" type="x-p"/> The reflexive נפרד has here the same meaning as the Rabbinical פּרשׁ מן־הצּבּוּר, to separate oneself from the congregation, <hi type="italic">Aboth</hi> ii. 5; נפרד denotes a man who separates himself, for he follows his own counsel, Arab. mnfrd (mtfrrd) brâyh, or jḥys almḥḥl (<hi type="italic">seorsum ab aliis secedens</hi>). Instead of לתּאוה, Hitzig, after Jerome, adopts the emendation לתאנה, “after an occasion” (a pretext), and by נפרד thinks of one pushed aside, who, thrown into opposition, seeks to avenge himself. But his translation of 1b, “against all that is fortunate he gnasheth his teeth,” shows how much the proverb is opposed to this interpretation. נפרד denotes one who willingly (Jdg 4:11), and, indeed, obstinately withdraws himself. The construction of יבקּשׁ with ל (also <reference osisRef="Job.10.6">Job 10:6</reference>) is explained by this, that the poet, giving prominence to the object, would set it forward: a pleasure (תאוה, as Arab. hawan, unstable and causeless direction of the mind to something, pleasure, freak, caprice), and nothing else, he goes after who has separated himself (Fl.); the effort of the separatist goes out after a pleasure, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the enjoyment and realization of such; instead of seeking to conform himself to the law and ordinance of the community, he seeks to carry out a separate view, and to accomplish some darling plan: <hi type="italic">libidinem sectatur sui cerebri homo</hi>. With this 1b accords. תּוּשׁיּה (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Prov.2.7">Pro 2:7</reference>) is concretely that which furthers and profits. Regarding התגּלּע, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at Pro 17:14. Thus putting his subjectivity in the room of the common weal, he shows his teeth, places himself in fanatical opposition against all that is useful and profitable in the principles and aims, the praxis of the community from which he separates himself. The figure is true to nature: the polemic of the schismatic and the sectary against the existing state of things, is for the most part measureless and hostile.
entries.b8885bfa4142369957e891510e45a41577d17498: <reference osisRef="Prov.18.2">Pro 18:2</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.18.2">2</reference> The fool hath no delight in understanding;    But only that his heart may reveal itself therein. <div eID="gen11308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11309" type="x-p"/> The verb חפץ forms the fut. יחפּץ as well as יחפּץ; first the latter from חפץ, with the primary meaning, to bow, to bend down; then both forms as intransitive, to bend oneself to something, to be inclined to something, Arab. 'ṭf. (Fl.). תּבוּנה is here the intelligence which consists in the understanding of one’s own deficiency, and of that which is necessary to meet it. The inclination of the fool goes not out after such intelligence, but (כּי אם־; according to Ben-Naphtali, כי־אם) only that his heart, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the understanding which he thinks that he already possesses, may reveal itself, show itself publicly. He thinks thereby to show himself in his true greatness, and to render a weighty service to the world. This loquacity of the fool, proceeding from self-satisfaction, without self-knowledge, has already, <reference osisRef="Prov.12.23">Pro 12:23</reference>, and often, been reprimanded.
entries.ecf763235637230dfb22d60c26813f1f41eb2dc8: <reference osisRef="Prov.18.3">Pro 18:3</reference> <div eID="gen11309" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11310" type="x-p"/> The group beginning with <reference osisRef="Prov.18.3">Pro 18:3</reference> terminates in two proverbs (<reference osisRef="Prov.18.6">Pro 18:6</reference> and <reference osisRef="Prov.18.7">Pro 18:7</reference>), related to the concluding verse of the foregoing: 3 If a godless man cometh, then cometh also contempt;    And together with disgrace, shame. <div eID="gen11310" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11311" type="x-p"/> J. D. Michaelis, and the most of modern critics, read רשׁע; then, contempt etc., are to be thought of as the consequences that follow godlessness; for that קלון means (Hitzig) disgracefulness, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, disgraceful conduct, is destitute of proof; קלון always means disgrace as an experience. But not only does the Masoretic text punctuate רשׁע, but also all the old translators, the Greek, Aramaic, and Latin, have done so. And is it on this account, because a coming naturally seems to be spoken of a person? The “pride cometh, then cometh shame,” <reference osisRef="Prov.11.2">Pro 11:2</reference>, was in their recollection not less firmly, perhaps, than in ours. They read רשׁע, because בוּז does not fittingly designate the first of that which godlessness effects, but perhaps the first of that which proceeds from it. Therefore we adhere to the opinion, that the proverb names the fiends which appear in the company of the godless wherever he goes, viz., first בוז, contempt (<reference osisRef="Ps.31.19">Psa 31:19</reference>), which places itself haughtily above all due subordination, and reverence, and forbearance; and then, with the disgrace [<hi type="italic">turpitudo</hi>], קלון, which attaches itself to those who meddle with him (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.18">Isa 22:18</reference>), there is united the shame, הרפּה (<reference osisRef="Ps.39.9">Psa 39:9</reference>), which he has to suffer from him who has only always expected something better from him. Fleischer understands all the three words in the passive sense, and remarks, “עם־קלון חרפה, a more artificial expression for קלון וחרפה, in the Turkish quite common for the copula wāw, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, swylh ṭbrâk, earth and water, 'wrtylh âr, the man and the woman.” But then the expression would be tautological; we understand בוז and חרפה of that which the godless does to others by his words, and קלון of that which he does to them by his conduct. By this interpretation, עם is more than the representative of the copula.
entries.1e786f53458a6c2c94572aedd71138e1c6b831b9: <reference osisRef="Prov.18.4">Pro 18:4</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.18.4">4</reference> Deep waters are the words from a man’s mouth,    A bubbling brook, a fountain of wisdom. <div eID="gen11311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11312" type="x-p"/> Earlier, we added to <hi type="italic">hominis</hi> the supplement <hi type="italic">sc. sapientis</hi>, but then an unnecessary word would be used, and that which is necessary omitted. Rather it might be said that אישׁ is meant in an ideal sense; but thus meant, אישׁ, like גּבר, denotes the valiant man, but not man as he ought to be, or the man of honour; and besides, a man may be a man of honour without there being said of him what this proverb expresses. Ewald comes nearer the case when he translates, “deep waters are the heart-words of many.” Heart-words - what an unbiblical expression! The lxx, which translates λόγος ἐν καρδίᾳ, has not read דברי לב, but דבר בלב (as <reference osisRef="Prov.20.5">Pro 20:5</reference>, עצה בלב־). But that “of many” is certainly not a right translation, yet right in so far as אישׁ (as at <reference osisRef="Prov.12.14">Pro 12:14</reference>) is thought of as made prominent: the proverb expresses, in accordance with the form of narrative proverbs which present an example, what occurs in actual life, and is observed. Three different things are said of the words from a man’s mouth: they are deep waters, for their meaning does not lie on the surface, but can be perceived only by penetrating into the secret motives and aims of him who speaks; they are a bubbling brook, which freshly and powerfully gushes forth to him who feels this flow of words, for in this brook there never fails an always new gush of living water; it is a fountain or well of wisdom, from which wisdom flows forth, and whence wisdom is to be drawn. Hitzig supposes that the distich is antithetic; מים עמקּים, or rather מי מעמקּים, “waters of the deep,” are cistern waters; on the contrary, “a welling brook is a fountain of wisdom.” But עמק means deep, not deepened, and deep water is the contrast of shallow water; a cistern also may be deep (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.22.14">Pro 22:14</reference>), but deep water is such as is deep, whether it be in the ocean or in a ditch. 4b also does not suggest a cistern, for thereby it would be indicated that the description, דברי פי־אישׁ, is not here continued; the “fountain of wisdom” does not form a proper parallel or an antithesis to this subject, since this much rather would require the placing in contrast of deep and shallow, of exhausted (drained out) and perennial. And: the fountain is a brook, the well a stream - who would thus express himself! We have thus neither an antithetic nor a synonymous (lxx after the phrase ἀναπηδῶν, Jerome, <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>., Luth.), but an integral distich before us; and this leads us to consider what depths of thought, what riches of contents, what power of spiritual and moral advancement, may lie in the words of a man.
entries.32582c5f8c22c857d8471a22197a2a61bf3e5f12: <reference osisRef="Prov.18.5">Pro 18:5</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.18.5">5</reference> To favour the person of the godless is not good,    And to oppress the righteous in judgment. <div eID="gen11312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11313" type="x-p"/> As <reference osisRef="Prov.18.4">Pro 18:4</reference> has one subject, so <reference osisRef="Prov.18.5">Pro 18:5</reference> has one predicate. The form is the same as Pro 17:26. שׂאת פּני (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.24.23">Pro 24:23</reference>), προσωποληψία, <hi type="italic">acceptio personae</hi>, is this, that one accepts the פני, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi> the personal appearance of any one (πρόσωπον λαμβάνει), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, regards it as acceptable, respectable, agreeable, which is a thing in itself not wrong; but in a judge who ought to determine according to the facts of the case and the law, it becomes sinful partiality. הטּות, in a forensic sense, with the accus. of the person, may be regarded in a twofold way: either as a turning aside, מדּין, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.2">Isa 10:2</reference>, from following and attaining unto the right, or as an oppression, for the phrase הטּה משׁפּט [to pervert justice] (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.17.23">Pro 17:23</reference>) is transferred to the person who experiences the oppression = perversion of the law; and this idea perhaps always underlies the expression, wherever, as <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Mal 3:5, no addition brings with it the other. Under <reference osisRef="Prov.17.15">Pro 17:15</reference> is a fuller explanation of לא־טוב.
entries.9a25e40a896af797d527b0990d739e73dd0a562b: <reference osisRef="Prov.18.6">Pro 18:6</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.18.6">6</reference> The lips of the fool engage in strife,    And his mouth calleth for stripes. <div eID="gen11313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11314" type="x-p"/> We may translate: the lips of the fool cause strife, for בּוא ב, to come with anything, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.66.13">Psa 66:13</reference>, is equivalent to bring it (to bring forward), as also: they engage in strife; as one says בּוא בדמים: to be engaged in bloodshed, 1Sa 25:26. We prefer this <hi type="italic">intrant</hi> (<hi type="italic">ingerunt se</hi>), with Schultens and Fleischer. יבאוּ for תּבאנה, a <hi type="italic">synallage generis</hi>, to which, by means of a “self-deception of the language” (Fl.), the apparent masculine ending of such duals may have contributed. The stripes which the fool calleth for (קרא ל, like <reference osisRef="Prov.2.3">Pro 2:3</reference>) are such as he himself carries off, for it comes <hi type="italic">a verbis ad verbera</hi>. The lxx: his bold mouth calleth for death (פיו ההמה מות יקרא); למהלמות has, in codd. and old editions, the <hi type="italic">Mem raphatum</hi>, as also at 19:29; the sing. is thus מהלוּם, like מנוּל to מנעליו, for the <hi type="italic">Mem dagessatum</hi> is to be expected in the inflected מהלם, by the passing over of the ō into ǔ.
entries.9acbcd4ace4e1b92b26f85e8524d504f8fb395c3: <reference osisRef="Prov.18.7">Pro 18:7</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.18.7">7</reference> The mouth of the fool is to him destruction,    And his lips are a snare to his soul. <div eID="gen11314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11315" type="x-p"/> As <reference osisRef="Prov.18.6">Pro 18:6</reference> corresponds to <reference osisRef="Prov.17.27">Pro 17:27</reference> of the foregoing group, so this <reference osisRef="Prov.18.7">Pro 18:7</reference> corresponds to Pro 17:28. Regarding מחתּה־לּו, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Pro 13:3. Instead of פי כּסיל, is to be written פּי־כסיל, according to <hi type="italic">Torath Emeth</hi>, p. 40, Cod. 1294, and old editions.
entries.052a73f199c7f5649fbc1c3343fa4187a33752f6: <reference osisRef="Prov.18.8">Pro 18:8</reference> <div eID="gen11315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11316" type="x-p"/> A pair of proverbs regarding the flatterer and the slothful: 8 The words of the flatter are as dainty morsels,    And they glide down into the innermost parts. <div eID="gen11316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11317" type="x-p"/> An “analogy, with an epexegesis in the second member” (Fl.), which is repeated in Pro 26:22. Ewald, Bertheau, Hitzig, and others, are constrained to interpret המו as introducing a contrast, and in this sense they give to מתלהמים all kinds of unwarrantable meanings. Ewald translates: a burning (להם, cogn. להב), and offers next: as whispering (להם, cogn. רעם, נהם); Ch. B. Michaelis, Bertheau, and others: as sporting (להם, cogn. להה); Hitzig: like soft airs (להם, cogn. Arab. hillam, <hi type="italic">flaccus, laxus</hi>). All these interpretations are without support. The word להם has none of all these significations; it means, as the Arab. lahima warrants, <hi type="italic">deglutire</hi>. But Böttcher’s explanation also: “as swallowed down, because spoken with reserve,” proceeds, like those others, from the supposed syntactically fine yet false supposition, that 8b is an antithetic “dennoch” [<hi type="italic">tamen</hi>]. In that case the poet would have written והם ירדים (cf. והוא, as the beginning of a conditional clause, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.29">Pro 3:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.23.3">Pro 23:3</reference>). But והוא, והם, with the finite following, introduces neither here nor at <reference osisRef="Deut.33.3">Deu 33:3</reference>; Jdg 20:34; <reference osisRef="Ps.95.10">Psa 95:10</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.43.23">Gen 43:23</reference>, a conditional clause. Thus 8b continues the clause 8a by one standing on the same line; and thus we do not need to invent a meaning for כמתלהמים, which forms a contrast to the penetrating into the innermost parts. The relation of the parts of the proverb is rightly given by Luther: <div eID="gen11317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11318" type="x-p"/> The words of the slanderer are stripes, <div eID="gen11318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11319" type="x-p"/> And they go through the heart of one. <div eID="gen11319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11320" type="x-p"/> He interprets להם as transposed from הלם (Rashi and others); but stripes cannot be called מתלהמים - they are called, 6b, מהלמות. This interpretation of the word has always more support than that of Symmachus: ὡς ἀκέραιοι; Jerome: <hi type="italic">quasi simplicia</hi>; Aquila, xxvi. 22: γοητικοί; which last, as also that of Capellus, Clericus, and Schultens: <hi type="italic">quasi numine quodam afflata</hi>, seems to support itself on the Arab. âhm iv. <hi type="italic">inspirare</hi>. But in reality âhm does not mean <hi type="italic">afflare</hi>; it means <hi type="italic">deglutire</hi>, and nothing else. The Jewish lexicographers offer nothing worth considering; Kimchi’s חלקים, according to which the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. translates μαλθακιζόμενοι, is fanciful; for the Talm. הלם, striking = hitting, suitable, standing well, furnishes no transition to “smooth” and “soft.” Immanuel compares âhm = בלע; and Schultens, who is followed by Gesenius and others, has already, with perfect correctness, explained: <hi type="italic">tanquam quae avidissime inglutiantur</hi>. Thus also Fleischer: things which offer themselves to be eagerly gulped down, or which let themselves be thus swallowed. But in this way can one be truly just to the <hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>.? The Arab. âlthm (stronger form, âltkm, according to which van Dyk translates mthl uḳam ḥlwt, like sweet morsels) means to swallow into oneself, which is not here appropriate. The <hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>. will thus have here a passive signification: things which are greedily swallowed. Regarding נרגּן from רגן, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at Pro 16:28. המו refers to the words of the flatterer, and is emphatic, equivalent to <hi type="italic">aeque illa, etiam illa</hi>, or <hi type="italic">illa ipsa</hi>. ירד is here connected with the obj. accus. (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.1.12">Pro 1:12</reference>) instead of with אל, Pro 7:27. חדרי, <hi type="italic">penetralia</hi>, we had already at <reference osisRef="Prov.7.27">Pro 7:27</reference>; the root-word is (Arab.) khdr, to seclude, to conceal, different from ḥdr, <hi type="italic">demittere</hi>, and ḥkhr (cogn. חזר), to finish, <hi type="italic">circumire</hi>. בּטן is the inner part of the body with reference to the organs lying there, which mediate not only the life of the body, but also that of the mind - in general, the internal part of the personality. The lxx does not translate this proverb, but has in its stead <reference osisRef="Prov.19.15">Pro 19:15</reference>, in a different version, however, from that it gives there; the Syr. and the Targ. have thereby been drawn away from the Hebr. text.
entries.ccf2b8de58a1fedc291b6d5618ec1760abc0440f: <reference osisRef="Prov.18.9">Pro 18:9</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.18.9">9</reference> He also who showeth himself slothful in his business,    Is a brother to him who proceedeth to destroy. <div eID="gen11320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11321" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>. התרפּה signifies here, as at <reference osisRef="Prov.24.10">Pro 24:10</reference>, to show oneself slack, lazy, negligent. מלאכה is properly a commission for another, as a king has a messenger, ambassador, commissioner to execute it; here, any business, whether an undertaking in commission from another, or a matter one engages in for himself. He who shows himself slack therein, produces in his way, viz., by negligence, destruction, as truly as the בּעל משׁחית, who does it directly by his conduct. Thus one is named, who is called, or who has his own delight in it, to destroy or overthrow. Jerome, incorrectly limiting: <hi type="italic">sua opera dissipantis</hi>. Hitzig well compares Mat 12:30. In the variation, <reference osisRef="Prov.28.24">Pro 28:24</reference>, the destroyer is called אישׁ משׁחית, the connection of the words being adject.; on the contrary, the connection of בעל משׁחית is genit. (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.22.24">Pro 22:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.23.2">Pro 23:2</reference>, etc.), for משׁחית as frequently means that which destroys = destruction. Von Hofmann (<hi type="italic">Schriftbew</hi>. ii. 2, 403) understands 'אישׁ מ of the street robber, 'בעל מ of the captain of robbers; but the designation for the latter must be 'שׂר מ, though at 1Ki 11:24 he is called by the name שׂר גּדוּד. The form of the word in the proverb here is more original than at 38:24. There חבר [companion] is used, here אח [brother], a general Semitic name of him who, or of that which, is in any way related to another, cf. Job 30:29. Fleischer compares the Arab. proverb: âlshbht âkht alkhṭyât, scepticism is the sister of sin.
entries.266206a1681ce0755877d0af413b23350502b3d4: <reference osisRef="Prov.18.10">Pro 18:10</reference> <div eID="gen11321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11322" type="x-p"/> Two proverbs, of the fortress of faith, and of the fortress of presumption: 10 A strong tower is the name of Jahve;      The righteous runneth into it, and is high. <div eID="gen11322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11323" type="x-p"/> The name of Jahve is the Revelation of God, and the God of Revelation Himself, the creative and historical Revelation, and who is always continually revealing Himself; His name is His nature representing itself, and therefore capable of being described and named, before all the <hi type="italic">Tetragramm</hi>, as the <hi type="italic">Anagramm</hi> of the overruling and inworking historical being of God, as the <hi type="italic">Chiffre</hi> of His free and all-powerful government in grace and truth, as the self-naming of God the Saviour. This name, which is afterwards interwoven in the name Jesus, is מגדּל־עז (<reference osisRef="Ps.61.4">Psa 61:4</reference>), a strong high tower bidding defiance to every hostile assault. Into this the righteous runneth, to hide himself behind its walls, and is thus lifted (<hi type="italic">perf. consec</hi>.) high above all danger (cf. ישׂגּב, <reference osisRef="Prov.29.25">Pro 29:25</reference>). רוּץ אל means, <reference osisRef="Job.15.26">Job 15:26</reference>, to run against anything, רוץ, <hi type="italic">seq. acc</hi>., to invest, blockade anything, רוץ בּ, to hasten within; Hitzig’s conjecture, ירוּם riseth up high, instead of ירוּץ, is a freak. רוץ בּ is speedily בוא בּ, the idea the same as <reference osisRef="Ps.27.5">Psa 27:5</reference>; Psa 31:21.
entries.37eae955bbe012fc1a1a4427b80455a55858d37a: <reference osisRef="Prov.18.11">Pro 18:11</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.18.11">11</reference> The possession of the righteous is his strong fort,      And is like a high wall in his imagination. <div eID="gen11323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11324" type="x-p"/> Line first = Pro 10:15. משׂכּית from שׂכה, Chald. סכה(whence after <hi type="italic">Megilla</hi> 14a, יסכּה, she who looks), R. שׂך, cogn. זך, to pierce, to fix, means the image as a medal, and thus also intellectually: image (conception, and particularly the imagination) of the heart (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.7">Psa 73:7</reference>), here the fancy, conceit; Fleischer compares (Arab.) tṣwwr, to imagine something to oneself, French <hi type="italic">se figurer</hi>. Translators from the lxx to Luther incorrectly think on שׂכך (סכך), to entertain; only the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. is correct in the rendering: ἐν φαντασίᾳ αὐτοῦ; better than Kimchi, who, after Ezr 8:12, thinks on the chamber where the riches delighted in are treasured, and where he fancies himself in the midst of his treasures as if surrounded by an inaccessible wall. <div eID="gen11324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11325" type="x-p"/> We place together <reference osisRef="Prov.18.12-Prov.18.19">Pro 18:12-19</reference>, in which the figure of a secure fortress returns:
entries.3f546401f478040f79168053a4d5e3561752b976: <reference osisRef="Prov.18.12">Pro 18:12</reference> <div eID="gen11325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11326" type="x-p"/> This proverb is connected with the preceding of the rich man who trusts in his mammon. <div eID="gen11326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11327" type="x-p"/> Before destruction the heat of man is haughty; <div eID="gen11327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11328" type="x-p"/> And humility goeth before honour. <div eID="gen11328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11329" type="x-p"/> Line first is a variation of <reference osisRef="Prov.16.18">Pro 16:18</reference>, and line second is similar to Pro 15:33.
entries.bdabb667db0418c5eba91769ea73467edfca6a80: <reference osisRef="Prov.18.13">Pro 18:13</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.18.13">13</reference> If one giveth an answer before he heareth,      It is to him as folly and shame. <div eID="gen11329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11330" type="x-p"/> The part. stands here differently from what it does at <reference osisRef="Prov.13.18">Pro 13:18</reference>, where it is subj., and at <reference osisRef="Prov.17.14">Pro 17:14</reference>, where it is pred. of a simple sentence; it is also here, along with what appertains to it in accordance with the Semitic idiom, subj. to 13b (one who answers ... is one to whom this...); but, in accordance with our idiom, it becomes a hypothetical antecedent. For “to answer” one also uses השׁיב without addition; but the original full expression is השׁיב דּבר, <hi type="italic">reddere verbum, referre dictum</hi> (cf. ענה דּבר, <reference osisRef="Jer.44.20">Jer 44:20</reference>, absol. in the cogn., <reference osisRef="Prov.15.28">Pro 15:28</reference>); דבר one may not understand of the word to which, but of the word with which, the reply is made. היא לו comprehends the meaning: it avails to him (<hi type="italic">ducitur ei</hi>), as well as it reaches to him (<hi type="italic">est ei</hi>). In Agricola’s <hi type="italic">Fünfhundert Sprüchen</hi> this proverb is given thus: <hi type="italic">Wer antwortet ehe er höret, der zaiget an sein torhait und wirdt ze schanden</hi> [he who answers before he hears shows his folly, and it is to him a shame]. But that would require the word to be יבושׁ, <hi type="italic">pudefiet</hi>; (היא לו) כּלמּה means that it becomes to him a ground of merited disgrace. “כּלמּה, properly wounding, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, shame (like <hi type="italic">atteinte à son honneur</hi>), from כּלם (cogn. הלם), to strike, hit, wound” (Fl.). Sirach Sirach(11:8) warns against such rash talking, as well as against the rudeness of interrupting others.
entries.0e0139c71cd2f810c51d1412c7643f0d9cc41ef9: <reference osisRef="Prov.18.14">Pro 18:14</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.18.14">14</reference> The spirit of a man beareth his sickness;      But a broken spirit, who can bear it? <div eID="gen11330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11331" type="x-p"/> The breath of the Creator imparting life to man is spoken of as <hi type="italic">spiritus spirans</hi>, רוּח (רוּח חיּים), and as <hi type="italic">spiritus spiratus</hi>, נפשׁ (נפשׁ חיּה); the spirit (<hi type="italic">animus</hi>) is the primary, and the soul (<hi type="italic">anima</hi>) the secondary principle of life; the double gender of רוח is accounted for thus: when it is thought of as the primary, and thus in a certain degree (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. p. 103ff.) the manly principle, it is mas. (<reference osisRef="Gen.6.3">Gen 6:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.51.12">Psa 51:12</reference>, etc.). Here the change of gender is in the highest degree characteristic, and אישׁ also is intentionally used (cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.15">1Sa 26:15</reference>) instead of אדם, 16a: the courageous spirit of a man which sustains or endures (כּלכּל R. כל, <hi type="italic">comprehendere, prehendere</hi>; Luther, “who knows how to contain himself in his sufferings;” cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.51.12">Psa 51:12</reference>, “may the free Spirit hold me”) the sickness [<hi type="italic">Siechthum</hi>] (we understand here “<hi type="italic">siech</hi>” in the old meaning = <hi type="italic">sick</hi>) with self-control, is <hi type="italic">generis masculini</hi>; while, on the contrary, the רוּח נכאה (as <reference osisRef="Prov.15.13">Pro 15:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.17.22">Pro 17:22</reference>), brought down from its manliness and superiority to disheartened passivity, is <hi type="italic">genere feminino</hi> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.51.12">Psa 51:12</reference> with <reference osisRef="Prov.18.19">Pro 18:19</reference>). Fleischer compares the Arab. proverb, thbât âlnfs bâlghdhâ thbât alrwh balghnâ, the soul has firmness by nourishment, the spirit by music.<note placement="foot">In the Arab. language, influenced by philosophy, rwh, the <hi type="italic">anima vitalis</hi>, and nfs, the <hi type="italic">anima rationalis</hi>, are inverted; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Baudissin’s <hi type="italic">Translationis antiquae Arab. libri Jobi quae supersunt</hi> (1870), p. 34.</note> <div eID="gen11331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11332" type="x-p"/> The question מי ישּׂאנּה is like <reference osisRef="Mark.9.50">Mar 9:50</reference> : if the salt becomes tasteless, wherewith shall one season it? There is no seasoning for the spice that has become insipid. And for the spirit which is destined to bear the life and fortune of the person, if it is cast down by sufferings, there is no one to lift it up and sustain it. But is not God the Most High the lifter up and the bearer of the human spirit that has been crushed and broken? The answer is, that the manly spirit, 14a, is represented as strong in God; the discouraged, 14b, as not drawing from God the strength and support he ought to do. But passages such as <reference osisRef="Isa.66.2">Isa 66:2</reference> do not bring it near that we think of the רוח נכאה as alienated from God. The spirit is נשׂא, the bearer of the personal and natural life with its functions, activities, and experiences. If the spirit is borne down to powerless and helpless passivity, then within the sphere of the human personality there is no other sustaining power that can supply its place.
entries.b66bda361f0a443a87d0ed74e2917ce920b04ce9: <reference osisRef="Prov.18.15">Pro 18:15</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.18.15">15</reference> The heart of a man of understanding gaineth knowledge,      And the ear of the wise seeketh after knowledge. נבון may be also interpreted as an adj., but we translate it here as at <reference osisRef="Prov.14.33">Pro 14:33</reference>, because thus it corresponds with the parallelism; cf. לב צדּיק, <reference osisRef="Prov.15.28">Pro 15:28</reference>, and לב חכם, <reference osisRef="Prov.16.23">Pro 16:23</reference>, where the adject. interpretation is excluded. The gaining of wisdom is, after <reference osisRef="Prov.17.16">Pro 17:16</reference>, referred to the heart: a heart vigorous in embracing and receiving it is above all necessary, and just such an one possesses the נבון, which knows how to value the worth and usefulness of such knowledge. The wise, who are already in possession of such knowledge, are yet at the same time constantly striving to increase this knowledge: their ear seeks knowledge, eagerly asking where it is to be found, and attentively listening when the opportunity is given of מצא, obtaining it.
entries.0ae80e0f61a79a263d238b3941a7a9bea384911b: <reference osisRef="Prov.18.16">Pro 18:16</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.18.16">16</reference> The gift of a man maketh room for him,      And bringeth him before the great. <div eID="gen11332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11333" type="x-p"/> That מתּן may signify intellectual endowments, Hitzig supposes, but without any proof for such an opinion. Intellectual ability as the means of advancement is otherwise designated, Pro 22:29. But Hitzig is right in this, that one mistakes the meaning of the proverb if he interprets מתן in the sense of שׂחד (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Prov.17.8">Pro 17:8</reference>): mtn is an indifferent idea, and the proverb means that a man makes free space, a free path for himself, by a gift, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, by this, that he shows himself to be agreeable, pleasing where it avails, not niggardly but liberal. As a proverb expresses it:<hi type="italic">Mit dem Hut in der Hand Kommt man durchs ganze Land</hi> [with hat in hand one goes through the whole land], so it is said here that such liberality brings before the great, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, not: furnishes with introductions to them; but helps to a place of honour near the great, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, those in a lofty position (cf. לפני, <reference osisRef="Prov.22.29">Pro 22:29</reference>; עם, <reference osisRef="Ps.113.8">Psa 113:8</reference>). It is an important part of practical wisdom, that by right liberality, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, by liberal giving where duty demands it, and prudence commends it, one does not lose but gains, does not descend but rises; it helps a man over the difficulties of limited, narrow circumstances, gains for him affection, and helps him up from step to step. The ā of מתּן is, in a singular way (cf. מתּנה, מתּנת), treated as unchangeable.
entries.8c0de40a4422afc5d3ae6b835adbfba2cd4ba78f: <reference osisRef="Prov.18.17">Pro 18:17</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.18.17">17</reference> He that is first in his controversy is right;      But there cometh another and searcheth him thoroughly - an exhortation to be cautious in a lawsuit, and not to justify without more ado him who first brings forward his cause, and supports it by reasons, since, if the second party afterwards search into the reasons of the first, they show themselves untenable. הראשׁון בּריבו are to be taken together; the words are equivalent to אשׁר יבא בריבו בראשׁונה: <hi type="italic">qui prior cum causa sua venit</hi>, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, <hi type="italic">eam ad judicem defert</hi> (Fl.). הראשׁון may, however, also of itself alone be <hi type="italic">qui prior venit</hi>; and בריבו will be taken with צדיק: <hi type="italic">justus qui prior venit in causa sua</hi> (<hi type="italic">esse videtur</hi>). The accentuation rightly leaves the relation undecided. Instead of יבא (יבא) the Kerı̂ has וּבא, as it elsewhere, at one time, changes the fut. into the perf. with ו (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Prov.20.4">Pro 20:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.6.21">Jer 6:21</reference>); and, at another time, the perf. with ו into the fut. (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.10.10">Psa 10:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.5.29">Isa 5:29</reference>). But here, where the <hi type="italic">perf. consec</hi>. is not so admissible, as <reference osisRef="Prov.6.11">Pro 6:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.20.4">Pro 20:4</reference>, the fut. ought to remain unchanged. רעהוּ is the other part, synon. with בעל דין חברו, <hi type="italic">Sanhedrin</hi> 7b, where the אזהרה לבית־דין (admonition for the court of justice) is derived from <reference osisRef="Deut.1.16">Deu 1:16</reference>, to hear the accused at the same time with the accuser, that nothing of the latter may be adopted beforehand. This proverb is just such an <hi type="italic">audiatur et altera pars</hi>. The <hi type="italic">status controversiae</hi> is only brought fairly into the light by the hearing of the <hi type="italic">altera pars</hi>: then comes the other and examines him (the first) to the very bottom. חקר, elsewhere with the accus. of the thing, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, ריב ,., thoroughly to search into a strife, <reference osisRef="Job.29.16">Job 29:16</reference>, is here, as at <reference osisRef="Job.28.11">Job 28:11</reference>, connected with the accus. of the person: to examine or lay bare any one thoroughly; here, so that the misrepresentations of the state of the matter might come out to view along with the reasons assigned by the accuser.
entries.9ff7f6f83c5d4f50e7a8a4bf9c74bfd07a062513: <reference osisRef="Prov.18.18">Pro 18:18</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.18.18">18</reference> The lot allayeth contentions,      And separateth between the mighty,<hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, erects a partition wall between them - those contending (הפריד בּין, as at 2Ki 2:11, cf. Arab. frḳ byn); עצוּמים are not opponents who maintain their cause with weighty arguments (עצּמות, <reference osisRef="Isa.41.21">Isa 41:21</reference>), <hi type="italic">qui argumentis pollent</hi> (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Rashi), for then must the truth appear in the <hi type="italic">pro et contra</hi>; but mighty opponents, who, if the lot did not afford a seasonable means of reconciliation, would make good their demands by blows and by the sword (Fl.). Here it is the lot which, as the judgment of God, brings about peace, instead of the <hi type="italic">ultima ratio</hi> of physical force. The proverb refers to the lot what the Epistle to the Heb; <reference osisRef="Heb.6.16">Heb 6:16</reference>, refers to the oath, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at Pro 16:33. Regarding מדינים and its altered forms, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., p. 145.
entries.94d2e70b16b3b4ab3ba49bb5071f41ae9661d010: <reference osisRef="Prov.18.19">Pro 18:19</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.18.19">19</reference> A brother toward whom it has been acted perfidiously resists more than a strong tower;      And contentions are like the bar of a palace. <div eID="gen11333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11334" type="x-p"/> Luther rightly regarded the word נושׁע, according to which the lxx, Vulg., and Syr. translated <hi type="italic">frater qui adjuvatur a fratre</hi>, as an incorrect reading; one would rather expect אח מושׁיע, “a brother who stands by,” as Luther earlier translated; and besides, נושׁע does not properly mean <hi type="italic">adjuvari</hi>, but <hi type="italic">salvari</hi>. His translation -<hi type="italic">Ein verletzt Bruder helt herter denn eine feste Stad</hi>,<hi type="italic">Und Zanck helt herter, denn rigel am Palast</hi> [a brother wounded resisteth more than a strong city, and strife resisteth more than bolts in the palace], is one of his most happy renderings. מקּרית־עז in itself only means ὑπὲρ πόλιν ὀχυράν (<hi type="italic">Venet</hi>.); the noun-adjective (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.10.10">Isa 10:10</reference>) to be supplied is to be understood to עז: עז הוּא or קשׁה הוא (Kimchi). The <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. נפשׁע occurs only here. If one reads נפשׁע, then it means one who is treated falsely = נפשׁע בּו, like the frequently occurring קמי, my rising up ones = קמים עלי, those that rise up against me; but Codd. (Also Baer’s <hi type="italic">Cod. jaman</hi>.) and old editions have נפשׁע, which, as we have above translated, gives an impersonal attributive clause; the former: <hi type="italic">frater perfidiose tractatus</hi> (Fl.: <hi type="italic">mala fide offensus</hi>); the latter: <hi type="italic">perfide actum est</hi>, <hi type="italic">scil</hi>. בּו <hi type="italic">in eum</hi> = <hi type="italic">in quem perfide actum</hi>. אח is, after <reference osisRef="Prov.17.17">Pro 17:17</reference>, a friend in the highest sense of the word; פשׁע means to break off, to break free, with ב or על of him on whom the action terminates. That the פּשׁע is to be thought of as אח of the אח נפשׁע is obvious; the translation, “brothers who break with one another” (Gesen.), is incorrect: אח is not collective, and still less is נפשׁע a <hi type="italic">reciprocum</hi>. The relation of אח is the same as that of אלּוּף, Pro 16:28. The Targum (improving the Peshito) translates אחא דמת עוי מן אחוי, which does not mean: a brother who renounces (Hitzig), but who is treated wickedly on the part of, his brother. That is correct; on the contrary, Ewald’s “a brother resists more than...” proceeds from a meaning of פשׁע which it has not; and Bertheau gives, with Schultens, an untenable<note placement="foot">Among the whole Heb. synon. for sinning, there exists no reflexive <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>.; and also the Arab. fsḳ has no ethical signification. נסכּל only, in the sense of fool, is found.</note> reflexive meaning to the <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. (which as denom. might mean “covered with crime,” <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. πλημμεληθείς), and, moreover, one that is too weak, for he translates, “a brother is more obstinate then....” Hitzig corrects אחז פּשׁע, to shut up sin = to hold it fettered; but that is not correct Heb. It ought to be עצר, כּבשׁ, or רדות. In 19a the force of the substantival clause lies in the מן (more than, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, harder = more difficult to be gained), and in 19b in the כּ; cf. Mic 7:4, where they are interchanged. The parallelism is synonymous: strifes and lawsuits between those who had been friends form as insurmountable a hindrance to their reconciliation, are as difficult to be raised, as the great bars at the gate of a castle (Fl.). The point of comparison is not only the weight of the cross-beam (from ברח, crosswise, across, to go across the field), but also the shutting up of the access. Strife forms a partition wall between such as once stood near each other, and so much thicker the closer they once stood. <div eID="gen11334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11335" type="x-p"/> With <reference osisRef="Prov.18.19">Pro 18:19</reference>, the series of proverbs which began with that of the flatterer closes. The catchword אח, which occurred at its commencement, 9b, is repeated at its close, and serves also as a landmark of the group following <reference osisRef="Prov.18.20">Pro 18:20</reference>-24. The proverb of the breach of friendship and of contentions is followed by one of the reaction of the use of the tongue on the man himself. <div eID="gen11335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11336" type="x-p"/> With <reference osisRef="Prov.18.19">Pro 18:19</reference>, the series of proverbs which began with that of the flatterer closes. entries.c14c5a5350865525952143879fa4935699730716: <reference osisRef="Prov.18.20">Pro 18:20</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.18.20">20</reference> Of the fruit which a man’s mouth bringeth is his heart satisfied;      By the revenue of his lips is he filled. <div eID="gen11336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11337" type="x-p"/> He will taste in rich measure of the consequences not merely of the good (<reference osisRef="Prov.12.14">Pro 12:14</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.13.2">Pro 13:2</reference>), but of whatever he has spoken. This is an oxymoron like <reference osisRef="Matt.15.11">Mat 15:11</reference>, that not that which goeth into the mouth, but that which cometh out of it, defileth a man. As at Joh 4:34 the conduct of a man, so here his words are called his βρῶμα. Not merely the conduct (<reference osisRef="Prov.1.31">Pro 1:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.3.10">Isa 3:10</reference>), but also the words are fruit-bringing; and not only do others taste of the fruit of the words as of the actions of a man, whether they be good or bad, but above all he himself does so, both in this life and in that which is to come.
entries.07aa7c6d949dd333aedbd5d9951f771642baa90f: <reference osisRef="Prov.18.21">Pro 18:21</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.18.21">21</reference> Death and life are in the power of the tongue;      And whoever loveth it shall eat its fruit. <div eID="gen11337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11338" type="x-p"/> The hand, יד, is so common a metaphor for power, that as here a hand is attributed to the tongue, so <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.47.14">Isa 47:14</reference> to the flame, and <reference osisRef="Ps.49.16">Psa 49:16</reference> to Hades. Death and life is the great alternative which is placed, <reference osisRef="Deut.30.15">Deu 30:15</reference>, before man. According as he uses his tongue, he falls under the power of death or attains to life. All interpreters attribute, 21b, ואהביה to the tongue: <hi type="italic">qui eam</hi> (<hi type="italic">linguam</hi>) <hi type="italic">amant vescentur</hi> (יאכל, distrib. sing., as <reference osisRef="Prov.3.18">Pro 3:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.35">Pro 3:35</reference>, etc.) <hi type="italic">fructu ejus</hi>. But “to love the tongue” is a strange and obscure expression. He loves the tongue, says Hitzig, who loves to babble. Euchel: he who guards it carefully, or: he who takes care of it, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, who applies himself to right discourse. Combining both, Zöckler: who uses it much, as εὐλογῶν or κακολογῶν. The lxx translates, οἱ κρατοῦντες αὐτῆς, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, אחזיה; but אחז means <hi type="italic">prehendere</hi> and <hi type="italic">tenere</hi>, not <hi type="italic">cohibere</hi>, and the tongue kept in restraint brings forth indeed no bad fruit, but it brings no fruit at all. Why thus? Does the suffix of ואהביה, perhaps like <reference osisRef="Prov.8.17">Pro 8:17</reference>, Chethı̂b, refer to wisdom, which, it is true, is not named, but which lies everywhere before the poet’s mind? At <reference osisRef="Prov.14.3">Pro 14:3</reference> we ventured to make חכמה the subject of 3b. Then 21b would be as a miniature of <reference osisRef="Prov.8.17">Pro 8:17</reference>-21. Or is ואהביה a mutilation of ואהב יהוה: and he who loves Jahve (<reference osisRef="Ps.97.10">Psa 97:10</reference>) enjoys its (the tongue’s) fruit?
entries.2b3722768574bb5f23f0a41fd6276ddc92c3e42a: <reference osisRef="Prov.18.22">Pro 18:22</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.18.22">22</reference> Whatso hath found a wife hath found a good thing,      And hath obtained favour from Jahve. <div eID="gen11338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11339" type="x-p"/> As ואהביה, 21b, reminds us of <reference osisRef="Prov.8.17">Pro 8:17</reference>, so here not only 22b, but also 22a harmonizes with <reference osisRef="Prov.8.35">Pro 8:35</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.12.2">Pro 12:2</reference>). A wife is such as she ought to be, as <reference osisRef="Prov.18.14">Pro 18:14</reference>, אישׁ, a man is such as he ought to be; the lxx, Syr., Targ., and Vulgate supply <hi type="italic">bonam</hi>, but “gnomic brevity and force disdains such enervating adjectives, and cautious limitations of the idea” (Fl.). Besides, אשׁה טובה in old Hebr. would mean a well-favoured rather than a good-dispositioned wife, which later idea is otherwise expressed, <reference osisRef="Prov.19.14">Pro 19:14</reference>; Pro 31:10. The <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. rightly has γυναῖκα, and Luther <hi type="italic">ein Ehefraw</hi>, for it is a married woman that is meant. The first מצא is <hi type="italic">perf. hypotheticum</hi>, Gesen. §126, <hi type="italic">Anm</hi>. 1. On the other hand, <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.26">Ecc 7:26</reference>, “I found, מוצא אני, more bitter than death the woman,” etc.; wherefore, when in Palestine one married a wife, the question was wont to be asked: או מוצא מצא, has he married happily (after מצא of the book of Proverbs) or unhappily (after מוצא of Ecclesiastes) (<hi type="italic">Jebamoth</hi> 63b)?<note placement="foot">Cf. Gendlau’s <hi type="italic">Sprichwörter u. Redensarten deutsch-jüdischer Vorzeit</hi> (1860), p. 235.</note> <div eID="gen11339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11340" type="x-p"/> The lxx adds a distich to <reference osisRef="Prov.18.22">Pro 18:22</reference>, “He that putteth away a good wife putteth away happiness; and he that keepeth an adulteress, is foolish and ungodly.” He who constructed this proverb [added by the lxx] has been guided by מצא to מוציא (Ezr 10:3); elsewhere ἐκβάλλειν (γυναῖκα), <reference osisRef="Gal.4.30">Gal 4:30</reference>, Sir. 28:15, is the translation of גּרשׁ. The Syr. has adopted the half of that distich, and Jerome the whole of it. On the other hand, <reference osisRef="Prov.18.23">Pro 18:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.18.24">Pro 18:24</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Prov.19.1-Prov.19.2">Pro 19:1-2</reference>, are wanting in the lxx. The translation which is found in some Codd. is that of Theodotion (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Lagarde).
entries.2afd1a2a8ab37abf7af4b598ddb92a8625849675: <reference osisRef="Prov.18.23">Pro 18:23</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.18.23">23</reference> The poor uttereth suppliant entreaties;      And the rich answereth rudenesses. <div eID="gen11340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11341" type="x-p"/> The oriental proverbial poetry furnishes many parallels to this. It delights in the description of the contrast between a suppliant poor man and the proud and avaricious rich man; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Samachschari’s <hi type="italic">Goldene Halsbänder</hi>, No. 58. תּחנוּנים, according to its meaning, refers to the <hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>. התחנּן, <hi type="italic">misericordiam alicujus pro se imploravit</hi>; cf. the old vulgar “barmen,” <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, to seek to move others to <hi type="italic">Erbarmen</hi> [compassion] (רחמים). עזּות, <hi type="italic">dura</hi>, from עז (synon. קשׁה), hard, fast, of bodies, and figuratively of an unbending, hard, haughty disposition, and thence of words of such a nature (Fl.). Both nouns are accus. of the object, as Job 40:27, תחנונים with the parallel רכּות. The proverb expresses a fact of experience as a consolation to the poor to whom, if a rich man insults him, nothing unusual occurs, and as a warning to the rich that he may not permit himself to be divested of humanity by mammon. A hard wedge to a hard clod; but whoever, as the Scripture saith, grindeth the poor by hard stubborn-hearted conduct, and grindeth his bashful face (<reference osisRef="Isa.3.15">Isa 3:15</reference>), challenges unmerciful judgment against himself; for the merciful, only they shall obtain mercy, αὐτοὶ ἐλεηθήσονται (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.7">Mat 5:7</reference>).
entries.c632c9d1bf96432dfe739034631145d2b0790bed: <reference osisRef="Prov.18.24">Pro 18:24</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.18.24">24</reference> A man of many friends cometh off a loser;      But there is a friend more faithful than a brother. <div eID="gen11341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11342" type="x-p"/> Jerome translates the commencing word by <hi type="italic">vir</hi>, but the Syr., Targ. by אית, which is adopted by Hitzig, Böttcher, and others. But will a German poet use in one line “<hi type="italic">itzt</hi>” [same as <hi type="italic">jetzt</hi> = now], and in the next “<hi type="italic">jetzt</hi>”? and could the Hebrew poet prefer to ישׁ its rarer, and her especially not altogether unambiguous form אישׁ (cf. to the contrary, <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.15">Ecc 7:15</reference>)? We write אישׁ, because the Masora comprehends this passage, with <reference osisRef="2Sam.14.19">2Sa 14:19</reference>; Mic 6:10, as the סבירין ישׁ 'ג, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, as the three, where one ought to expect ישׁ, and is thus exposed to the danger of falling into error in writing and reading; but erroneously אשׁ is found in all these three places in the <hi type="italic">Masora magna</hi> of the Venetian Bible of 1526; elsewhere the Masora has the <hi type="italic">defectiva scriptio</hi> with like meaning only in those two other passages. While אישׁ = ישׁ, or properly ישׁ, with equal possibility of אשׁ,<note placement="foot">One sees from this interchange how softly the י was uttered; cf. Wellhausen’s <hi type="italic">Text der B. Samuel</hi> (1871) (Preface). Kimchi remarks that we say אקטל for אקטל, because we would otherwise confound it with יקטל.</note> and it makes no material difference in the meaning of 24a whether we explain: there are friends who serve to bring one to loss: or a man of many friends comes to loss, - the <hi type="italic">inf</hi>. with ל is used in substantival clauses as the expression of the most manifold relations, Gesen. §132, <hi type="italic">Anm</hi>. 1 (cf. at <reference osisRef="Hab.1.17">Hab 1:17</reference>), here in both cases it denotes the end, as <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.92.8">Psa 92:8</reference>, to which it hastens with many friends, or with the man of many friends. It is true that אישׁ (like בּעל) is almost always connected only with genitives of things; but as one says אישׁ אלהים: a man belongs to God, so may one also say אישׁ רעים: a man belongs to many friends; the common language of the people may thus have named a man, to whom, because he has no definite and decided character, the rule that one knows a man by his friends is not applicable, a so-called every-man's-friend, or all-the-world's-friend. Theodotion translates ἀνὴρ ἑταιριῶν τοῦ ἑταιρεύσασθαι; and thus also the Syr., Targ., and Jerome render (and among the moderns, Hitzig) התרעע as reflexive in the sense of to cherish social intercourse; but this reflexive is התרעה, Pro 22:24. That התרועע is either <hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>. of רוּע, to exult, <reference osisRef="Ps.60.10">Psa 60:10</reference>; 65:14, according to which the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. translates (contrary to Kimchi) ὥστε ἀλαλάζειν: such an one can exult, but which is not true, since, according to 24b, a true friend outweighs the many; or it is <hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>. of רעע, to be wicked, sinful (Fl.: <hi type="italic">sibi perniciem paraturus est</hi>); or, which we prefer, warranted by <reference osisRef="Isa.24.19">Isa 24:19</reference>, of רעע, to become brittle (Böttcher and others) - which not only gives a good sense, but also a similar alliteration with רעים, as <reference osisRef="Prov.3.29">Pro 3:29</reference>; Pro 13:20. In contradistinction to רע, which is a general, and, according to the usage of the language (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, 17b), a familiar idea, the true friend is called, in the antithetical parallel member, אהב (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.6">Pro 27:6</reference>); and after <reference osisRef="Prov.17.17">Pro 17:17</reference>, דּבק מאח, one who remains true in misfortune. To have such an one is better than to have many of the so-called friends; and, as appears from the contrast, to him who is so fortunate as to have one such friend, there comes a blessing and safety. Immanuel has given the right explanation: “A man who sets himself to gain many friends comes finally to be a loser (סופו להשּׁבר), for he squanders his means, and is impoverished in favour of others.” And Schultens: <hi type="italic">At est amicus agglutinatus prae fratre. Rarum et carum esse genus insinuatur, ac proinde intimam illam amicitiam, quae conglutinet compingatque corda, non per multos spargendam, sed circumspecte et ferme cum uno tantum ineundam</hi>. Thus closes this group of proverbs with the praise of friendship deepened into spiritual brotherhood, as the preceding, <reference osisRef="Prov.18.19">Pro 18:19</reference>, with a warning against the destruction of such a relation by a breach of trust not to be made good again.  <chapter eID="Prov.18"/> <div eID="gen11342" type="x-p"/>
